cloud2trees Species Validation George Woolsey 14 October, 2026 1 Introduction The cloud2trees R package provides a framework for generating single-tree forest inventories from aerial point cloud data. The pipeline consolidates workflows to process raw point clouds, identify individual trees, and extract or model tree-level structural attributes including location, height, diameter at breast height (DBH), and crown base height (CBH). Because aerial point clouds lack the spectral information typically used to identify tree species natively, species-level information within the cloud2trees framework is currently a critical gap. To address this limitation, this analysis evaluates a novel, computationally efficient workflow designed to predict tree species by fusing point cloud structural data with the USFS TreeMap data product. TreeMap is a raster map of imputed FIA plot identifiers at 30-meter spatial resolution for the conterminous United States, which can be used to link with FIA-measured tree list data. This FIA tree list data is already used in cloud2trees to build site-specific allometric equations to predict DBH from tree height using the trees of the TreeMap imputed plots. 1.1 Proposed Species Classification Method The proposed workflow will use the imputed FIA plot lists from the 30-meter TreeMap raster product that fall within the extent of the point cloud being evaluated. Because the TreeMap data product is a raster of imputed plots for a given area at 30m resolution, we should not assume that the tree list of an imputed plot represents the actual trees present at that location with complete accuracy. Instead, we expect the TreeMap imputed plots to be more accurate as we look over a broader area with accuracy decreasing at smaller scales. That is, when we consider the tree composition of an entire forest stand we expect TreeMap to generally get the main species and forest type correct but for each 30m raster cell we expect it to be less accurate within a single cell, potentially being a completely incorrect representation of the actual ground setting. As such, we’ll weight the individual tree records based on the stability of the imputed plots looking over a window surrounding the focal cell. Specifically, we’ll calculate the proportion of surrounding cells (5x5) that share the same imputed plot identifier as the focal cell and use this weight as a measure of TreeMap’s predicted stability to place less weight on plots that occur infrequently and more weight on plots that occur frequently. To train the predictive model, trees from the selected FIA lists are assigned to their respective cell centers. Their coordinates are then spatially jittered within the 30-meter pixel boundary. This jittering breaks up the artificial grid lines of the raster data, creating a continuous spatial surface while preserving the broader species distribution trends. Using the FIA tree list data, we’ll build an ensemble of Random Forest species classification models trained on tree height and spatial coordinates. Because tree species is a categorical variable, we’ll generate a single prediction for each tree from the model ensemble using a majority voting system to output the final species prediction for each point cloud-derived tree. 1.2 Validation Data and Accuracy Evaluation To test this proposed species classification method, we compiled a collection of validation datasets across diverse forest conditions for this specific analysis project. These datasets consist of coincident aerial point cloud data (including USGS 3DEP ALS, UAS-lidar, and UAS-SfM) paired with field-measured stem maps or plot inventories where species identities are known. We’ll evaluate the species classification method using two approaches: Individual Tree-Level Accuracy This approach evaluates classification accuracy at the individual tree level. It maps every predicted tree species against the reference field-measured tree using a classical confusion matrix cross-tabulation. Given that our analysis is focused on evaluating the proposed taxonomic classification algorithm (rather than the individual tree detection method), we’ll evaluate the taxonomic classification accuracy conditionally for successfully detected tree crowns (true positive matches). This conditional evaluation will allow us to isolate taxonomic classification performance from tree detection errors. The confusion matrix will allow us to calculate class-specific performance metrics, including producer’s accuracy (omission error) and user’s accuracy (commission error) and overall accuracy. Site-Wide Compositional Accuracy Instead of evaluating trees one by one, this accuracy evaluation aggregates the species counts or proportions across an entire plot or forest stand. It then calculates the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index to compare the predicted species composition against the observed field composition. The index returns a value between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates identical species compositions and 1 indicates completely non-overlapping communities. Because Bray-Curtis is a dissimilarity measure, it can be interpreted as: \[\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{dissimilarity} \approx 1-\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{similarity}\] The Bray-Curtis index is a widely trusted metric in community ecology. Dissimilarity/similarity metrics tell us how well the proposed method captures the overall ecological community structure. Even if individual tree predictions are misaligned, the proposed method may still capture the correct stand-level abundance proportions, which can still be valuable for management. 1.3 Benefits and Next Steps Integrating species identification directly into the cloud2trees framework would enable the direct assignment of individual tree species (or genus) before modeling secondary biophysical attributes (e.g., DBH, CrBH, CrBD) which could improve tree-level precision (Weiskittel et al., 2011) and management decisions that require consideration of individual tree species for removal and retention during silvicultural treatment design or in modeling tree-level fire effects. Ultimately, these methods could enable the integration of species-specific allometries and fire behavior parameters at scale, supporting management needs where explicit tree-level species identification is less critical. Species-Specific Allometry: Attaching species to the point cloud-derived tree list enables the application of targeted allometric equations such as those currently used to predict DBH from tree height. Biomass and Volume Mapping: Attaching species to the point cloud-derived tree list allows individual tree metrics to feed directly into the National Scale Volume Biomass (NSVB) equations and total tree and tree component biomass based on existing allometries. These equations require species information alongside structural dimensions to model merchantable timber volume, total aboveground biomass, and tree component (e.g. stem, crown) biomass.

This includes many steps. Utilize multiple window functions for ITD Evaluate detection accuracy with segmentation matching of the predicted crowns with the field reference points Select the best performing window function with the ITD result used for the remaining species method validation Species/Genus Prediction: Predict species for the point cloud-generated tree list Tree-level Species/Genus Evaluation: Evaluate the tree-level accuracy of the proposed classification method Site-level Species/Genus Evaluation: Evaluate the site-level accuracy of the proposed classification method based on proportional distributions 3.1 Field Data Field data from this study site is from: Andrew Hudak, Seth Bigelow, Nuria Sánchez-López, and Vanessa Niemczyk. 2025. Field measurements of coarse wood, duff, litter, and trees for the Eglin Air Force Base 2023 fuels campaign. Wildland Fire Science Initiative (WFSI) https://doi.org/10.60594/W4RG6P Field measurements collected before and after 2023 study fires at Eglin Air Force Base (AFB) to document fuel loads (large diameter fuels, litter depth, duff depth) and trees in a 3-year rough in sandhill longleaf pine, and the effects of study fires on these variables. Fuel loads, which were measured along transects, were co-located with tree observations, which were measured within fixed-radius plots. These field observations were also co-located with three-dimensional fuel and laser scan plots to allow for leveraging of these other data. After the study fires in March 2023, trees within 10 m of plot center were identified to functional group (pine, hardwood or species), measured for diameter at breast height with a diameter tape, measured for distance from outer bark to plot center, and measured for azimuth from plot center to tree. Some post-processing was done using lidar scans to distinguish between evergreeen and deciduous hardwoods. Saplings were tallied by ordinal quadrant (up to 5 m from plot center). Tree measurements were not taken in unit L25. In unit G20, plots HH01, HH02, HH03, HH04, HH05 were sampled pre-fire but not post fire. In unit G25, plots HH105, HH95, PP16 were sampled pre-fire but not post fire. according to Eglin_2022_Tree_and_Transect_Field_Protocol.pdf, the post-fire sampling protocol for trees was: I. Determine if plot radius is 8 or 11.3 meters and record on datasheet a. If there are 4 or more trees within an 8-meter radius, then the plot radius is 8-meters. b. If there are 0 to 3 trees within an 8-meter radius, then increase the plot radius to 11.3-meters. II. Sample all trees ≥10 cm DBH within the plot radius and over from plot center III. Sample all pine saplings ONLY ≥2.5 to 10 cm DBH by recording: a. Radius (4 or 5.6m): i. If tree sampling radius was 8-meters, then sapling sampling radius = 4-meters ii. If tree sampling radius was 11.3-meters, then sapling sampling radius = 5.6-meters b. Quadrant = NE, SE, SW, or NW c. Count = How many of the same species in that quadrant d. Species = Longleaf pine (Pinus palustris), Loblolly pine (Pinus taeda), Sand pine (Pinus clausa) or TBD for those interested, pre- and post-burn photographs for each plot were archived here: https://doi.org/10.60594/W4GW2T # pred_trees_list 3.4 Species/Genus Prediction Method for some context of the primary objective of this analysis, here is what we said in the cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 3.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in cloud2trees::trees_dbh() # let's make a function to standardize this process since we'll be using it in more than one `cloud2trees::trees_*` function now treemap_data_loader <- function(sf_poly, input_treemap_dir = NULL) { #################################################################### # check external data #################################################################### # find external data find_ext_data_ans <- cloud2trees:::find_ext_data( input_treemap_dir = input_treemap_dir ) # if can't find external treemap data if(is.null(find_ext_data_ans$treemap_dir)){ stop(paste0( "Treemap data has not been downloaded to package contents. We expect the TreeMap imputed plots to be more accurate as we look over a broader area with accuracy decreasing at smaller scales. That is, when we consider the tree composition of an entire forest stand we expect TreeMap to generally get the main species and forest type correct but for each 30m raster cell (i.e. the plot location that we get the X and Y coordinates for the tree list used for training from) we expect it to be less accurate with a cell potentially being a completely incorrect representation of the actual ground setting. As such, we we weight the individual tree records based on the stability of the imputed plot id’s looking over a window surrounding the focal cell (stability_weight in treemap_trees_spatial_df). This conditional evaluation will allow us to isolate taxonomic model performance from tree detection errors (reviewed above here). In practice, the ITD window function would be tuned for the specific site and data being analyzed, but we implemented an automated ITD window selection process here since we will be evaluating many different sites and forest types. we’re going to use the tree-level prediction and reference data for all TP (true positive) predictions to perform confusion matrix accuracy evaluation of the species predictions. using the confusion matrix evaluation we’ll calculate the following metrics: Overall Accuracy: Measures the global percentage of all correctly classified trees out of the entire dataset of true positive (TP) observations. Provides an overall summary metric but can mask performance on uncommon species. User’s Accuracy (precision): Measures the reliability of specific predicted species. For example, if the method predicts a tree is a ponderosa pine, how often it is actually true. Producer’s Accuracy (recall): Measures how well the model successfully aligns with what was measured on the ground. For example, out of all real ponderosa pine trees measured in the field, what percentage did the method correctly identify. \[\text{Overall Accuracy} = \frac{\text{Number of Correctly Classified Species Observations}}{\text{Total Number of Successfully Detected Trees (TPs)}}\] \[\text{User's Accuracy (Species } i\text{)} = \frac{\text{Number of Correctly Classified Observations for Species } i}{\text{Total Number of Predicted Observations for Species } i}\] \[\text{Producer's Accuracy (Species } i\text{)} = \frac{\text{Number of Correctly Classified Observations for Species } i}{\text{Total Number of Reference Observations for Species } i}\] let’s make a function to get the confusion matrix and those accuracy metrics # This metric compares the proportional compositions of each species predicted by the model against the reference proportions within a defined area or site. Instead of evaluating trees one by one, this accuracy evaluation aggregates the species counts or proportions across an entire plot or forest stand. The Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index is used to compare the predicted species composition against the observed field composition. The index returns a value between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates identical species compositions and 1 indicates completely non-overlapping communities. Because Bray-Curtis is a dissimilarity measure, it can be interpreted as: \[\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{dissimilarity} \approx 1-\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{similarity}\] The Bray-Curtis index is a widely trusted metric in community ecology. Dissimilarity/similarity metrics tell us how well the proposed method captures the overall ecological community structure. Even if individual tree predictions are misaligned, the proposed method may still capture the correct stand-level abundance proportions, which can still be valuable for management. What it means for this evaluation: Even if individual-level classification accuracy is low, the model may still achieve acceptable aggregate composition accuracy. Real-World Ecological Application: This aggregate evaluation is valuable for large-scale forest structure measurement including: timber management, carbon and fuel assessments, and landscape ecology patterns. If a forestry manager only needs to know the total volume, fuel loading, or biomass ratios of species across a broad area or management unit to write a management plan, they don’t care if individual tree predictions are slightly off. They care about aggregate community structure which makes Bray-Curtis (and other similiarity/dissimilarity metrics) more relevant than overall, producer’s, and user’s accuracy. let’s make a function to use the full prediction and reference data irrespective of instance matching status to calculate the aggregated species composition metrics similarity_tree_class_fn <- function( pred_trees , ref_trees , use_genus = F ) { # here is what we said in the cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 4.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in here is what we said in the cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 5.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in Softmax model) tree species will be our dependent variable and the most simple model will use tree height and tree location (X and Y coordinates) as independent variables. The training FIA tree list data (identified from the TreeMap imputed plots of the area of interest) includes tree height and we’ll use the centroid of the TreeMap 30m raster cell to represent the individual tree X and Y location (i.e. each tree within the same cell will have the same coordinate). here is what we said in the cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 6.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in here is what we said in the cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 7.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in cloud2trees manuscript (a draft of the manuscript which may be different than what was actually published): However, taxonomic differentiation using airborne lidar alone remains one of the most technically challenging aspects of forest inventory workflows (White et al., 2016, 2025; Fassnacht et al., 2024). In practice, genus-level distinction is often more realistic when relying on remote sensing and supplemental spatial data (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). As a practical, computationally efficient approach, future research could evaluate predicting tree-level species or genus for potential integration into cloud2trees by leveraging supplemental spatial datasets. Testing could evaluate either using tree lists from FIA plots linked through a spatial overlay with TreeMap (Houtman et al., 2025) to train a taxonomic classification model based on structural and competition metrics shared between FIA and cloud2trees tree lists, or by proportionally assigning species using BigMap species-level proportional biomass raster data (Wilson et al., 2012, 2018). Incorporating finer-scale taxonomic classification than the currently implemented FIA forest type groups into the cloud2trees tree list will enable the integration of detailed biomass equations such as the National Scale Volume Biomass system (NSVB; Westfall et al., 2024) and other allometries that require species- or genera-level information (e.g., Réjou‐Méchain et al., 2017; Gonzalez‐Akre et al., 2022). cloud2trees does not currently include functionality to attach species to it’s tree list. there are a few paths forward for performing species-specific workflows with the cloud2trees tree list: the proposed method which we are evaluating presently, will predict tree-level species using the TreeMap imputed FIA plot tree list to build a species classification model based on height and tree location to attach tree species to our tree list. The model will inherently account for the proportional distribution of different species. early testing of the proposed method used a bayesian hierarchical model grouped by imputed FIA plot identifier that allows the intercept and the slope of height to vary by plot took quite a while to run for a relatively small area (~20-30 mins). as such, we are going to use a random forest (RF) classifier to enable more computationally efficient classification. cloud2trees already implements random forest models to model missing HMD and CBH values that were not successfully extracted from the point cloud and uses a model averaging method that subsamples the training data (to reduce model fit times), estimates the model several times with different subsamples, then model averages the predictions. Because the species is not a metric variable that can be averaged, we’ll use the same method but employ a model majority voting system instead. we can do this with some of the cloud2trees built-in functionality. ultimately, if the proposed species/genera classification method achieves decent accuracy results, it could be integrated into the cloud2trees framework as cloud2trees::trees_species(), for example. this function would take an input spatial tree list and attach the predicted species/genera 8.4.1 Training Data load in the TreeMap data and clip to our trees as in variable and the most simple model will use tree height and tree location (X and Y coordinates) as independent variables. Considering the combined tree height and spatial location via a full interaction model (i.e. height*x*y) allows the model to capture how the species-height relationship varies across space. let’s estimate the RF using data subsampling and model averaging for a computationally efficient way to get estimates over broad areas with potentially large tree lists. 9 Taxonomic Classification Accuracy Summary

9 Taxonomic Classification Accuracy Summary Now that we have completed the analysis and processing of the proposed species classification method for our collection of validation datasets, let’s summarize the achieved accuracy in one place. As a reminder, here is what we did: We compiled a collection of validation datasets across diverse forest conditions. These datasets consist of coincident aerial point cloud data (including USGS 3DEP ALS, UAS-lidar, and UAS-SfM) paired with field-measured stem maps or plot inventories where species identities are known. We evaluated our proposed species classification method using two approaches: Individual Tree-Level Accuracy This approach evaluates classification accuracy at the individual tree level. It maps every predicted tree species against the reference field-measured tree using a classical confusion matrix cross-tabulation. Given that our analysis is focused on evaluating the proposed taxonomic classification algorithm (rather than the individual tree detection method), we’ll evaluate the taxonomic classification accuracy conditionally for successfully detected tree crowns (true positive matches). This conditional evaluation will allow us to isolate taxonomic classification performance from tree detection errors. The confusion matrix will allow us to calculate class-specific performance metrics, including producer’s accuracy (omission error) and user’s accuracy (commission error) and overall accuracy. Site-Wide Compositional Accuracy Instead of evaluating trees one by one, this accuracy evaluation aggregates the species counts or proportions across an entire plot or forest stand. It then calculates the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity index to compare the predicted species composition against the observed field composition. The index returns a value between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates identical species compositions and 1 indicates completely non-overlapping communities. Because Bray-Curtis is a dissimilarity measure, it can be interpreted as: \[\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{dissimilarity} \approx 1-\textrm{Bray-Curtis}_{similarity}\] The Bray-Curtis index is a widely trusted metric in community ecology. Dissimilarity/similarity metrics tell us how well the proposed method captures the overall ecological community structure. Even if individual tree predictions are misaligned, the proposed method may still capture the correct stand-level abundance proportions, which can still be valuable for management. The metrics we will be looking at in this review are: Evaluation Level Metric Name Succinct Metric Description Species-Level Evaluation Genus-Level Evaluation Individual Tree Level Accuracy(Taxonomic Classification Power) Overall Accuracy (OA) Proportion of correctly classified species/genera among successfully detected trees (TP matches). ✓ ✓ Site-Wide Compositional Accuracy(Stand Inventory Performance) Bray-Curtis Dissimilarity Proportion of absolute species/genus abundance mismatched. ✓ ✓ Bray-Curtis Similarity Proportion of absolute species/genus abundance matching perfectly. ✓ ✓ Proportional RMSE Average percentage deviation error margin per species/genus. ✓ ✓ Accuracy metrics were evaluated at both the species and genus taxonomic levels to quantify the accuracy trade-offs associated with pushing the classification method to the finest taxonomic level (species). We anticipate classification performance at the genus level to be higher than at the species level because aggregating predictions into broader taxonomic groups inherently reduces the number of classification classes, increasing the mathematical probability of a correct match. An acceptable level of classification accuracy at the genus-level can still be valuable in operational forestry settings. Species within the same genus frequently occupy similar ecological functional roles, and distinguishing between them represents one of the most persistent challenges when relying on remote sensing datasets alone (Vauhkonen et al., 2014b). Furthermore, members of the same genus typically exhibit similar growth forms and structural geometries, which mitigates species-level misclassifications when using volumetric equations. From an operational management perspective, individual species-level distinction within a genus, such as separating blue spruce (Picea pungens) from Engelmann spruce (Picea engelmannii), for example, often yields marginal practical benefit if their allometries and ecological roles remain functionally similar. If the primary management objective requires highly accurate species-level classification at the individual tree level, then our proposed approach is likely to be insufficient and unreliable.
